raw_response:
For your workflow—paste a YouTube link, keep several useful passages, join them into a shorter study video, and download the result—I would start with Kapwing or Flixier if their free limits are sufficient. For regular or longer editing, a free desktop workflow is yt-dlp followed by LosslessCut.

## 1. Kapwing: a direct browser option for short summaries

[Kapwing's YouTube trimmer](https://www.kapwing.com/tools/trim/youtube) describes splitting, trimming and rearranging clips in a timeline. Its [official tutorial](https://www.kapwing.com/resources/how-to-edit-someone-elses-youtube-video/) describes importing a YouTube link and exporting a downloadable edited video.

The practical workflow is to import the video, split around each passage you want to keep, remove unwanted portions and gaps, arrange the remaining clips, then export and download. This fits the study-summary task without requiring a desktop editor.

The significant restriction is the free export allowance. The [current pricing page](https://www.kapwing.com/pricing) lists a four-minute maximum exported video, 720p resolution and a watermark. It is therefore a suitable candidate if each finished digest is short and the watermark is acceptable.

## 2. Flixier: another browser option, with a monthly allowance

[Flixier's cutting documentation](https://flixier.com/tools/cut-videos) explicitly says it can import a pasted YouTube link directly into the cloud. It also explains cutting and trimming on the timeline, combining clips, and exporting to your computer. You can use that sequence to assemble the important sections into one study video.

Its [current free plan](https://flixier.com/pricing) includes ten minutes of video export per month, 720p output, 2 GB of storage and a watermark. The monthly export allowance could suit occasional short summaries; it is restrictive if you intend to process many lectures.

## 3. Free desktop workflow: yt-dlp plus LosslessCut

If the browser allowances are too restrictive, use these two tools together:

- [yt-dlp](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp) handles downloading from the YouTube URL. It is a command-line tool with official desktop downloads, not a visual editor. Its documentation and indexed source also describe timestamp-based section downloads with FFmpeg, but downloading alone does not assemble your finished digest.
- [LosslessCut](https://github.com/mifi/lossless-cut) handles the visual selection and joining work. Its README documents cutting video, merging retained segments, and exporting without re-encoding. It provides free manual downloads for Windows, macOS and Linux.

The workflow is to save the source using yt-dlp, open that local video in LosslessCut, mark the sections you want to retain, and merge those sections when exporting. LosslessCut is aimed at fast rough cutting, and its lossless merging requires compatible codecs; sections from a single source are the natural starting point. This is a two-tool workflow rather than a single application with a YouTube import button.

I would choose Kapwing for an occasional digest of four minutes or less, compare Flixier if its monthly allowance fits better, and choose the desktop pair for repeated study-video editing.

### Evidence and date limits

These are documentation-based candidates; I did not upload a video or test an export. Kapwing has an official tutorial dated May 7, 2020, which provides pre-July-2023 evidence for the basic import/edit/download workflow. The pricing figures above come from live pages checked during this run, so they should not be read as verified July 2023 plan terms. The other candidates' cited feature pages are current, and attempts to retrieve historical yt-dlp and LosslessCut README versions failed. Their exact relevant feature sets at the question's date therefore remain unverified.
